title: API Keys and Basic Authentication
subtopics: API keys and their intended use cases
learning_outcomes: Explain how api keys and basic authentication affects an API contract or implementation.
Apply the key ideas from api keys and their intended use cases to a concrete API example.
Identify one failure, security, or compatibility risk and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on api keys and basic authentication in authentication, authorization, and identity. You will connect api keys and their intended use cases to a concrete API contract decision, inspect a small example, and decide what evidence proves the behavior is correct.
content.why_it_matters: API Keys and Basic Authentication matters because API consumers depend on predictable behavior even when clients, servers, networks, and stored data evolve independently. Applying api keys and their intended use cases deliberately reduces ambiguity, makes failures easier to diagnose, and gives tests a clear expectation.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: A credential may identify a caller; policy checks decide whether that caller can perform this operation on this resource. In this lesson, treat “API Keys and Basic Authentication” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.

content_blocks.title: Concepts to connect
items: API keys and their intended use cases

content_blocks.title: Inspect the pattern: API Keys and Basic Authentication
content_blocks.code:
GET /v1/profile HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.test
Authorization: Bearer <short-lived-access-token>
Accept: application/json

# The server validates token signature/issuer/audience/expiry,
# then checks the caller's permission for this specific resource.
content_blocks.expected_output: A valid token authenticates a caller but does not automatically authorize every action or resource.

content_blocks.title: Walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with “API keys and their intended use cases”; it establishes the vocabulary for this topic. Next, compare it with “Key storage, rotation, and revocation” and “Limitations of long-lived shared credentials”. In a real API, write down the observable behavior first, then test one normal request and one invalid or unauthorized request. Keep resource state, caller identity, and internal implementation details separate.

content_blocks.title: Professional review check
content_blocks.text: Authentication establishes identity; authorization must still check the requested action and resource. The worked snippet is intentionally inspectable, not an executable hosted API. Replace example.test and placeholder identifiers with local test data only when you implement the lesson project.

content.reset_steps: Use a disposable local database or test fixture for implementation work. Restore seed data between runs; never point exercises at production customer data or live payment endpoints.
troubleshooting: Check the exact HTTP method, path, status, header, media type, and payload before changing implementation code.
Separate a transport failure from an application validation failure, authorization denial, and dependency/database failure.
Confirm the example and its client tooling version are compatible; consult the linked standard or official guidance when behavior is ambiguous.
common_mistakes: Treating api keys and basic authentication as an implementation detail rather than a documented behavior.
Testing only the happy path and ignoring malformed, unauthorized, conflicting, duplicate, or dependency-failure cases.
Publishing an example without checking version assumptions, sensitive-data exposure, and the expected output.
